justice: Most street space is allocated to mixed vehicle movement and curbside parking, while a clearly separated pedestrian sidewalk is largely absent, indicating uneven spatial distribution among road users.
Cars and vans are parked along both sides of the narrow lane, reducing effective public space for pedestrians and cyclists and limiting fair sharing of the corridor.
No visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or designated accessible pedestrian route can be identified near the building edge or tree side, weakening barrier-free accessibility for diverse users.
safety: The street is narrow and appears to mix cars, parked vehicles, and a scooter in the same carriageway, increasing conflict risk among road users.
There is no visible marked crosswalk, speed hump, bike lane, or other traffic-calming element in the scene, so safety relies largely on informal driver behavior.
Parked vehicles along the curb and the large trees on the left may reduce sightlines, making it harder for drivers and riders to detect other users entering the roadway.
livability: The mature tree canopy on the left adds greenery and gives the lane a calmer residential feel, which supports basic neighborhood livability.
The street frontage is mostly blank residential walls with barred windows and little active ground-floor use, so social interaction and street vitality appear limited.
Clutter near the right building edge, including stored items and rough frontage conditions, reduces the sense of orderly everyday public space.
sustainability: Large roadside trees provide ecosystem benefits such as shade, cooling, and some stormwater interception, which positively support environmental performance.
The lane design appears car-oriented with multiple parked motor vehicles and no visible public transport stop or protected cycling facility, limiting support for low-carbon travel choices.
There are no visible permeable paving areas, rain gardens, or other green stormwater features; most of the surface appears hard and sealed.
aesthetics: The dense green tree canopy creates the strongest visual quality in the scene and softens the otherwise hard street environment.
Building facades on the right are plain and utilitarian, with visible air-conditioning units, wires, and security bars that reduce architectural appeal.
Surface wear, patched pavement, and miscellaneous items placed along the building frontage weaken the overall visual neatness of the streetscape.
comfort: The trees on the left provide substantial shade, improving thermal comfort for anyone walking or standing along that side of the street.
Physical comfort is reduced because there is no clearly paved, continuous pedestrian sidewalk separated from moving or parked vehicles.
Psychological comfort is moderate to low since the narrow shared lane, close parked cars, and scooter presence can make users feel exposed to traffic conflicts.
walkability: A dedicated sidewalk is not clearly visible; pedestrians would likely need to share space with vehicles or walk along uneven edges near buildings and parked cars.
The right edge of the street shows rough pavement, patching, and frontage clutter, which can interrupt a comfortable and continuous walking path.
Although the tree canopy improves shade and environmental quality, the lack of pedestrian infrastructure such as crossings, buffers, and wayfinding keeps overall walkability low.
bikeability: There is no visible bike lane, shared-lane marking, or any dedicated cycling facility, so cyclists must ride directly in mixed traffic.
The narrow carriageway and curbside parked vehicles increase the risk of close passing and dooring conflicts for people cycling.
No bicycle parking, bike signage, or intersection treatments are visible, indicating weak support for convenient and safe everyday cycling.
